title: The acquittal–legal certainty paradox
subtitle: Context, jury discretion, and speech liability under section 12 of the Terrorism Act 2000
summary: An acquittal tells you that one defendant was not convicted on one charge, on the evidence in that trial. It does not, by itself, tell everyone else whether the same words would be lawful in their mouths. This study sets out three different thresholds — legality, prosecutability and adjudication — and walks a structured thought experiment comparing the Greenstein case with a hypothetical typical speaker, without inviting anyone to repeat the words.
jurisdiction: England and Wales / United Kingdom / European Convention on Human Rights
scope: A legal study of what a Crown Court acquittal does and does not settle, and of lawful ways to seek a reasoned ruling. It is not legal advice, not a prediction of any verdict, and not an invitation to publish the words discussed.
status_note: Checked 27 November 2026. Trial transcripts and the judge’s directions in R v Greenstein have not been obtained. No public Attorney General’s Reference arising from that acquittal has been located in this review. The thought experiment is analysis, not a finding. No Freedom of Information requests have been made for this review.

sections.title: The question this page is asking
sections.intro: A law-abiding citizen can be left unsure of the rules even after a widely reported acquittal. The public interest in knowing where the criminal law draws the line on speech is real. Repeating charged words in order to test that line is not a safe or sufficient way to find out.

entries.title: A deproscription application, and a narrower speech question
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: On 26 November 2026, Al Jazeera reported that the Jewish Network for Palestine had that day submitted an application to the Home Secretary, under section 4 of the Terrorism Act 2000, to deproscribe Hamas. The report said the filing came five years to the day after Hamas was fully proscribed in the United Kingdom, and that the Home Secretary, Shabana Mahmoud, has 90 days beginning the day after the application is received. Section 4 requires regulations to fix a period for determination. Regulation 7 of the 2006 Regulations sets that period at 90 days beginning with the day after receipt, which matches the figure in the report. If the application is refused, section 5 of the Act gives the applicant a right of appeal to the Proscribed Organisations Appeal Commission. Al Jazeera reported that the group can appeal a refusal; it did not name the Commission in the body of the article.

paragraphs.text: The same report returned to Tony Greenstein, a Jewish anti-Zionist activist and writer, then 72, who had been prosecuted after publishing material on 7 October 2023. Press Association reporting, carried by The Jewish Chronicle, records that a Kingston Crown Court jury acquitted him on 21 August 2026 of inviting support for Hamas. It was an acquittal, not a hung jury. The report identifies him as the son of an Orthodox rabbi. He is not reported to be a rabbi himself. Al Jazeera quoted him on the chilling effect of the Hamas ban and described the charge as having been brought in November 2024.

sources.locator: Greenstein comments, November 2024 charge, August 2026 acquittal
Kingston acquittal, age, background and verdict date

paragraphs.text: The question that follows is narrower than deproscription, and it is the subject of this page. An acquittal establishes that a particular defendant has not been convicted of a particular offence on the evidence in that trial. It does not necessarily establish that the words used are lawful for everyone, in every context. A 40-year-old non-Jewish Polish man who used the same words, on the same date, on the same platform, would not automatically inherit that result. The Crown Prosecution Service, applying the Full Code Test, assesses whether an impartial, properly directed jury would be more likely than not to convict on the evidence in the new case. If a previous acquittal of comparable words lowers that assessment, there may be no charge and therefore no new judicial ruling. If there is a charge, another unreasoned jury verdict still may not produce a binding statement of the general law. How, then, can a law-abiding person obtain an authoritative court ruling on the boundary without first risking a terrorism prosecution?

sections.title: Three thresholds that are not the same question
sections.intro: Part of the confusion comes from treating legality, charging and a jury verdict as if they were a single switch.

entries.title: Legality, prosecutability and adjudication
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: Legality is a question about the statute and its interpretation by appellate courts: do the words and surrounding circumstances satisfy the elements of an offence? Prosecutability is a question for the Crown Prosecution Service under the Full Code Test: is there a realistic prospect of conviction, and is a prosecution required in the public interest? Adjudication, in a Crown Court trial on indictment, is a question for the jury: are they sure that every element is proved? A case which does not pass the evidential stage must not proceed, no matter how serious or sensitive it may be. A realistic prospect means that an objective, impartial and reasonable jury, properly directed, is more likely than not to convict. That is a different, and lower, threshold than the criminal standard of proof, which requires the court to be sure of guilt. A jury verdict of not guilty does not usually come with reasons, so it often leaves open which element failed.

sources.locator: Evidential stage, paras 4.6–4.7; public interest, paras 4.9–4.10

sections.title: The Greenstein case, as reported
sections.intro: The comparison only works if the baseline is stated carefully, including what the prosecution actually put before the jury and what remains unseen.

paragraphs.text: Press Association reporting records that a Kingston Crown Court jury acquitted Tony Greenstein on a single count of inviting support for Hamas. The count concerned three posts published on 7 October 2023 and material linked from them. The jury was out for two hours and eleven minutes. The same reporting identifies him as a Jewish activist and writer, aged 72 at trial, and the son of an Orthodox rabbi. His position, as reported, was that he did not support Hamas as an organisation, even though he held strong views about the events of 7 October 2023. The prosecution material, as reported, included praise for the attack in a linked blog. Al Jazeera later described a blog titled “Full Support for the Gaza Ghetto Uprising” and said he was charged in November 2024 under section 12 for inviting support “on the basis of one sentence in that blog and for writing ‘please share’.” The two accounts are consistent in outline and differ in emphasis. This review has not inspected the indictment, the posts as exhibited, or the linked article as used at trial, so the precise charging text remains a matter of those reports.

sources.locator: Single count, three posts, linked material, 2 hours 11 minutes, defence and prosecution positions
Blog title, November 2024 charge, ‘please share’ and one sentence in the blog

paragraphs.text: The phrase most often repeated in later discussion is “Full support for the Gaza ghetto uprising.” Isolated from the posts and the linked blog, that slogan is an incomplete account of what the jury was asked to consider. A fair comparison with another speaker has to start from the publication as alleged, not from a five-word extract.

sources.locator: Posts and linked blog as the subject-matter of the count
‘Please share’ and the blog sentence as described in later reporting

paragraphs.text: The case is already recorded in the speech-offences register, which should be read alongside this study. Press Association reporting also recorded that the trial judge considered, and then declined to pursue, a contempt issue arising from the defendant’s closing address, describing that speech in terms that referred to his age. That exchange was about contempt of court. It is not a judicial finding that age caused the acquittal, and it does not tell us which element of the offence the jury rejected. We have not obtained the trial transcript or the legal directions.

sources.locator: Acquittal reporting; contempt issue arising from the closing address

sections.title: Two different offences under section 12
sections.intro: Section 12 contains more than one offence. The reported Greenstein charge was inviting support. A later or different prosecution could, in principle, be put on another subsection. An acquittal on one does not automatically decide the other.

paragraphs.text: Section 12(1) makes it an offence to invite support for a proscribed organisation, other than support that is, or is restricted to, the provision of money or other property. In R v Choudary and Rahman, decided on 22 March 2016, the Court of Appeal treated “invite” and “support” as ordinary English words which a jury can understand without elaborate definition. The prosecution must prove that the organisation was proscribed; that the defendant used words which in fact invited support for that organisation; and that the defendant knew at the time that he was inviting support for that proscribed organisation. Knowledge that the organisation was proscribed is part of what must be proved. The court also accepted that the word “invite” itself connotes a mental element: it is difficult to see how an invitation could be inadvertent. What the court did not require was proof that the defendant himself supported the organisation, intended to support it, or invited others to join him in providing support. The criminality lies in inviting support from third parties.

sources.locator: Section 12(1)
Paras 41–49: ordinary meaning; knowledge; invitation not inadvertent; no need to prove the defendant’s own support

paragraphs.text: The same judgment is careful to distinguish an invitation of support from the mere holding or expression of personal beliefs, or an invitation to someone else to share an opinion or belief. That distinction is often the whole of a difficult case. It is also why context — surrounding words, a linked article, timing, and the way a message would reasonably have been understood — can matter without any need to treat the speaker’s religion or nationality as an element of the offence.

sources.locator: Para 49: invitation of support distinguished from mere expression of belief

entries.title: Section 12(1A): expressing a supportive opinion while reckless as to encouragement

paragraphs.text: Section 12(1A) was inserted by section 1 of the Counter-Terrorism and Border Security Act 2019 and came into force on 12 April 2019. It is a different offence. It is committed where a person expresses an opinion or belief that is supportive of a proscribed organisation, and is reckless as to whether a person to whom the expression is directed will be encouraged to support that organisation. The maximum sentence on indictment for the section 12 offences is 14 years’ imprisonment. That maximum was substituted on 29 June 2021 by section 26 of the Counter-Terrorism and Sentencing Act 2021. It was not created by the 2019 Act, which inserted subsection (1A) while the previous 10-year maximum still applied.

sources.locator: Section 12(1A) and the current maximum
Insertion of section 12(1A), in force 12 April 2019
14-year maximum substituted 29 June 2021

paragraphs.text: In R v ABJ and BDN [2026] UKSC 8, decided on 26 February 2026, the Supreme Court considered section 12(1A) and article 10 of the Convention. The appeals were brought on certified points of law before trial, and were unanimously dismissed. Lord Reed, with whom the other justices agreed, summarised the ingredients of the offence at paragraph 82. The defendant must have expressed an opinion or belief; that opinion or belief must be objectively supportive of the organisation, judged by how the words would naturally and reasonably have been understood in the circumstances; the defendant must have known that the opinion or belief was supportive of the organisation; the organisation must then have been proscribed; there must have been a risk that a person to whom the expression was directed would be encouraged to support that organisation; the defendant must have known of that risk; and it must have been objectively unreasonable to take that risk in the circumstances known to the defendant. Recklessness is the two-limb test in R v G: awareness of the risk, and unreasonableness in taking it. The Court also held that “directed” imports an intention that the words be read or heard; a post on public social media is directed to anyone who reads it.

sources.locator: Paras 75–83: ingredients of section 12(1A); recklessness; “directed”
Article 10, freedom of expression

paragraphs.text: On article 10, the Court rejected the contention that, once the ingredients are proved, a trial court or jury must carry out a further, separate assessment of whether conviction would be a proportionate interference with freedom of expression. Paragraphs 135 to 139 explain why. Proportionality had already been assessed by the government in bringing forward the 2019 Act, by Parliament in enacting it, and by the courts in the appeal itself. The function of the trial court is to determine whether the ingredients set out in paragraph 82 have been proved to the criminal standard. Compatibility with Convention rights is a question of law, not a question of fact for the jury. The judge must still withdraw a case on which a reasonable jury could not be sure, and must ensure that any sentence is proportionate. ABJ and BDN were not a trial of Greenstein’s words, and they concerned subsection (1A), not the inviting-support offence reported in his case. They do, however, place a substantial obstacle in the way of a general article 10 attack on section 12(1A).

sources.locator: Paras 135–139: no separate trial-court proportionality assessment; compatibility is a question of law

entries.title: Political or “just cause” framing is not a statutory defence

paragraphs.text: Two earlier authorities are relevant to any argument that words such as “uprising” or “resistance” fall outside the terrorism legislation because of the speaker’s political or moral framing. In R v Gul, the Supreme Court held that the definition of terrorism in section 1 of the 2000 Act is broad and contains no exemption for armed attacks on state or coalition forces during an armed conflict. In R v F, the Court of Appeal held that there is no “just cause” or tyrannical-regime exception built into the Act. Motive or perceived moral justification does not, by itself, take conduct outside the statutory language. Those holdings do not decide whether any particular post invited support or expressed a supportive opinion. They do show why a speaker’s own description of events as resistance is not a complete answer once the statutory elements are in play.

sources.locator: No armed-conflict exemption in the section 1 definition of terrorism

sections.title: A thought experiment, not a mock prosecution
sections.intro: What follows is a structured comparison, on paper, of two speakers. It is not a prediction. It is not a finding. It is not an invitation to anyone to publish the words discussed, to invite a charge, or to test the Crown Prosecution Service. The point of the exercise is to show which questions the law actually asks, and which differences are legally irrelevant.

entries.title: Person A and Person B
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: Person A is Tony Greenstein, as reported: a 72-year-old Jewish anti-Zionist activist and writer, the son of an Orthodox rabbi, who was tried at Kingston Crown Court on a count of inviting support for Hamas and acquitted on 21 August 2026. Person B is a hypothetical 40-year-old non-Jewish Polish man who, on the same date and on the same kind of platform, published the same words — meaning, so far as the reports allow, the posts and the linked blog material that formed the subject of the count, not a detached slogan. The question can be put plainly, and even a little casually: the dude was 72 and Jewish — might that have influenced the jury? We are monitoring the situation. It is a fair question to ask in public. It is not evidence that those facts caused the acquittal. Age, nationality, ethnicity and religion are not elements of section 12, and they are not a lawful ground for treating two speakers differently.

sources.locator: Person A’s reported profile, charge and acquittal
Identity is not an ingredient of either subsection

paragraphs.text: There is, however, a legitimate distinction that has nothing to do with identity. The reporting records that the court heard evidence of Greenstein’s earlier published criticism of Hamas, and that he argued “congratulating” Hamas was a figure of speech, while maintaining that he did not support Hamas as an organisation. A hypothetical Person B, imagined only as a typical speaker of the same words on the same day, would not automatically have that publication history, those surrounding statements, or that body of evidence. Context of that kind can be relevant to whether words amounted to an invitation, and to whether the speaker knew they were inviting support. Treating that evidence as relevant is not the same thing as treating Jewish identity, or age, as a reason for a different result.

entries.title: Walking the statutory elements
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: On a section 12(1) charge, the same legal questions would be asked of both speakers. Was Hamas a proscribed organisation at the time? Did the words, taken in their circumstances, in fact invite support for Hamas? Did the speaker know, at the time, that he was inviting support for that proscribed organisation? A judge would be likely to direct a jury, in line with Choudary, that “invite” and “support” bear their ordinary meaning; that an invitation is not accidental; that the speaker need not himself support the organisation or invite others to join him; and that merely holding or expressing a belief, or inviting someone to share an opinion, is not enough. We do not have the directions actually given in Greenstein, so this is a statement of the appellate law, not a reconstruction of that summing-up.

sources.locator: The elements and the likely shape of a direction
Section 12(1)

paragraphs.text: On a section 12(1A) charge — which was not the reported Greenstein charge, but which a later prosecutor might consider — the questions would follow paragraph 82 of ABJ and BDN. Was an opinion or belief expressed? Would those words naturally and reasonably have been understood, in the circumstances, as supportive of Hamas? Did the speaker know that? Was there a risk that a person to whom the expression was directed would be encouraged to support Hamas? Did the speaker know of that risk, and was it objectively unreasonable to take it? The jury would not be asked to carry out a separate article 10 proportionality assessment. The judge would still have to decide whether the evidence was capable of making a reasonable jury sure of each ingredient.

sources.locator: Para 82 ingredients; paras 135–139, no separate jury proportionality assessment
Section 12(1A)

paragraphs.text: At the charging stage, the Full Code Test would be applied to Person B on the evidence actually available in that case. A previous acquittal of another person is relevant to the prosecutor’s assessment of how an impartial jury might view comparable words, but it does not automatically take a new case below the evidential threshold. Each case is considered on its own facts. If the evidential stage is not met, the case must stop there. If it is met, the prosecutor still has to ask whether a prosecution is required in the public interest. The Code does not exist in order to obtain a test-case ruling for the benefit of public debate, and a desire for legal clarity is not, by itself, a reason to charge someone.

entries.title: What this experiment can and cannot show
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: The honest conclusion is limited, and it should stay limited. We cannot say that Person B would be convicted, or acquitted, or not charged. Unreasoned jury verdicts cannot be replayed. In England and Wales, section 20D of the Juries Act 1974 makes it an offence intentionally to disclose, solicit or obtain information about statements made, opinions expressed, arguments advanced or votes cast by members of a jury in the course of their deliberations in the proceedings. The older prohibition in section 8 of the Contempt of Court Act 1981 was repealed for England and Wales by the Criminal Justice and Courts Act 2015. It is therefore not possible, and not lawful, to settle this question by asking the Greenstein jury why it acquitted. Controlled research about juries in general is a different thing from reopening a particular trial. This review has not relied on any such study, because a live official text of the often-cited Ministry of Justice paper was not verified in this pass.

sources.locator: Offence of disclosing, soliciting or obtaining jury deliberation information
The actual verdict remains unexplained in the public reports

paragraphs.text: What can be said is this. The legally relevant questions are the same for both speakers. Identity should be irrelevant to the legal test, even if, as a hypothesis, a jury’s perception of a defendant might be influenced by age, manner or background. There is no evidence that Greenstein’s Jewish identity, or his age, caused the acquittal. A hypothetical Person B might still face a different evidential picture because the surrounding publication, or the absence of a long record of criticism of Hamas, would not be the same. An acquittal on section 12(1) would not, in any event, decide a section 12(1A) charge. The plausible outcome range for Person B therefore includes no investigation, no charge, a charge and an acquittal, or a charge and a conviction. This page does not pick one. Repeating the words in public in order to force a ruling would not reliably produce a reasoned precedent, and it would put the speaker at risk of prosecution. That is not a route this study recommends or invites.

sections.title: The prosecutorial paradox
sections.intro: The Full Code Test can leave a citizen without either a prosecution or a ruling, and a prosecution still may not produce a precedent.

entries.title: Why a previous acquittal does not automatically close, or open, the next case
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: The observation that started this study is a real institutional tension, not a trick of wording. A citizen wants to know whether particular words are criminal. A comparable defendant has been acquitted. When the Crown Prosecution Service assesses a new case, a previous acquittal may reduce the assessed prospect of conviction. If the evidential stage is not met, there is no prosecution and no judicial determination. If it is met, and the public-interest stage is also met, the result is another fact-specific trial, which may end in another unexplained verdict. Neither path necessarily produces a binding statement of the general law. The important qualification is that one previous acquittal does not automatically drive a new case below the charging threshold. The Code requires an assessment of the evidence in that case, including any defence the suspect may rely on. Equally, the Service’s function is to decide whether to prosecute on the tests in the Code, not to supply advisory rulings so that public debate can be conducted with certainty.

sources.locator: Paras 4.6–4.10: evidential stage, own facts, public interest; the Code is a charging test, not an advisory jurisdiction

sections.title: The awareness paradox
sections.intro: There is a paradox inside the paradox. Once Person B knows the Greenstein case, the charging tests, and the ways a defendant’s circumstances may have been perceived, that knowledge cannot be unlearned. Citing the acquittal is not a defence. Deliberate, informed repetition of the same words is not the same experiment.

entries.title: A prior acquittal is not a defence, and it is rarely evidence
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: If Person B were ever on trial, the instinctive plea — “but Tony Greenstein was acquitted for the same words” — does not answer the charge. An acquittal decides that particular defendant’s case. It does not declare the words lawful for everyone, and a jury verdict creates no precedent. The plea that a person has already been acquitted protects that acquitted person on that charge. It does not travel with the words to a later speaker.

sources.locator: A different defendant’s earlier verdict is, in principle, only that jury’s opinion

paragraphs.text: The leading statement is in Hui Chi-ming v The Queen. The Privy Council held that a defendant was not entitled to adduce evidence of another person’s earlier acquittal, because “the verdict reached by a different jury (whether on the same or different evidence) in the earlier trial was irrelevant and amounted to no more than evidence of the opinion of that jury.” The Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) has restated the general rule in England and Wales: generally speaking, evidence of the outcome of an earlier trial arising out of the same events is irrelevant and therefore inadmissible, since it is no more than the opinion of that earlier jury. There are narrow exceptions, for example where an acquittal is said to bear on the credibility of a confession or of a prosecution witness. Those exceptions are about the fairness of related proceedings, not about using someone else’s unexplained verdict as proof that a phrase is lawful. The Greenstein verdict, reached on different evidence about a different speaker and without public reasons, sits even further from that territory.

sources.locator: Different jury’s verdict is irrelevant: no more than that jury’s opinion
Para 22: general rule, and the limited exceptions

entries.title: Why awareness cannot simply be parked at the door
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: The colourful name suggested for this further twist — a quantum meta shape-shifting entangled paradox — is a way of stating a simpler point. Ignorance of the surrounding circumstances might have left Person B closer, in appearance, to a one-off speaker of the same words. Awareness cannot be put back in the bottle. Person B now knows, or could be shown to know, that the words were prosecuted as an invitation of support for Hamas; that the count was not confined to a detached slogan; that Greenstein’s age, Jewish identity and earlier published criticism of Hamas formed part of how the case was reported; and that the Crown Prosecution Service asks whether a realistic prospect of conviction exists, and whether a prosecution is required in the public interest. He cannot honestly recast himself as Greenstein, or replay Greenstein’s evidence, merely by repeating the words.

sources.locator: The reported charge, the surrounding publication, and the contextual evidence in that trial
The Full Code Test that a later, informed speaker can be shown to know

paragraphs.text: The legally interesting question is not whether that knowledge is “too woke” or “too meta.” It is whether it could affect the inferences a jury is asked to draw about mental state and purpose. Under section 12(1), the prosecution must prove that the defendant knew, at the time, that he was inviting support for a proscribed organisation. Under section 12(1A), the prosecution must prove knowledge that the opinion or belief was supportive of the organisation, and recklessness as to encouragement: awareness of a risk that a person to whom the expression was directed would be encouraged to support that organisation, and that it was objectively unreasonable to take that risk. Might deliberate repetition of words already prosecuted, by a speaker who has studied the earlier case, make it easier to infer that knowledge, or that awareness of risk? Might a jury also be invited to ask what the repetition was for? Those are questions about how evidence may be assessed. They are not a finding that awareness converts an otherwise lawful statement into a crime, and they are not a reason to publish the words in order to test the point.

sources.locator: Section 12(1): knowledge that the defendant was inviting support for a proscribed organisation
Section 12(1A): knowledge, and recklessness as awareness of risk plus objective unreasonableness
The two offences

paragraphs.text: The inference can also run the other way, and it should be stated equally plainly. Knowing the legal ingredients more clearly might, in some framings, support an argument that the speaker was trying to stay on the lawful side of the line: for example, by avoiding language of invitation, by making clear that a comment was a personal opinion, or by declining to encourage anyone to support a proscribed organisation. Recklessness is not made out merely because a risk was known; the taking of the risk must also have been objectively unreasonable in the circumstances known to the defendant. Better legal knowledge is therefore not automatically aggravating, and it is not automatically exculpatory. It is part of the circumstances. The safe conclusion remains the one already reached: this is not a puzzle to be solved by repeating the words.

sources.locator: The second limb of recklessness: unreasonableness in the circumstances known to the defendant
Mere expression of belief, or an invitation to share an opinion, is distinguished from inviting support

entries.title: Freedom of Information, as a sideline
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: A lawful way of asking for more official transparency, without generating a new defendant, is a request under the Freedom of Information Act 2000. Public authorities, including the Home Office, the Crown Prosecution Service and police forces such as the Metropolitan Police, are under a duty to communicate recorded information they hold, subject to cost limits and exemptions. Some of the numbers that matter are already published. The Home Office series “Operation of police powers under the Terrorism Act 2000” is official statistics on arrests, outcomes and stop and search in Great Britain. The latest release, published on 8 October 2026, covers the period to 30 June 2026 and is the final quarterly edition; the series is moving to a six-monthly schedule. The commentary records that, of arrests in the year ending June 2026, 704 had so far resulted in a charge, including 634 under section 12 or section 13 linked to supporting Palestine Action. Those figures are aggregated across two sections and are dominated, in that year, by Palestine Action-linked cases. The release does not isolate Hamas-related speech cases. The CPS itself points to the Home Office series for arrest and prosecution numbers, and does not publish official statistics of its own.

sources.locator: The general right of access to recorded information held by a public authority

CPS statement that terrorism arrest and prosecution numbers are published by the Home Office

paragraphs.text: FOI can still be useful for figures or documents that are not in those releases: for example, a count of section 12 arrests, charges, no-further-action decisions and outcomes, broken down by subsection, or charging guidance that is not already on the public record. A published CPS FOI response dated 1 June 2025 said the Service had commenced 11 prosecutions under section 12(1A) between 7 October 2023 and 7 October 2024 inclusive, in England and Wales, from manual records described as provisional and not official statistics. That is an illustration of what a narrow request can yield, not a complete map of section 12. This review has not made its own FOI requests.

sources.locator: 11 prosecutions under s.12(1A), 7 October 2023 to 7 October 2024; provisional manual records

paragraphs.text: Requests often fail, or come back heavily redacted, for reasons set out in the Act. Section 12 permits a refusal where the authority estimates that the cost of compliance would exceed the appropriate limit, prescribed as £600 for authorities listed in Part I of Schedule 1 to the Act (broadly, central government) and £450 for other public authorities, including police forces. Among the exemptions most likely to be considered for terrorism-related material, section 23 is an absolute exemption for information supplied by, or relating to, listed security bodies. Section 24 is a qualified exemption, subject to a public-interest test, where exemption is required for the purpose of safeguarding national security. Section 30 covers information held for criminal investigations or proceedings, and section 31 covers prejudice to law enforcement where section 30 does not apply; both are qualified. Section 40 protects personal data, and is absolute in the cases provided for by section 2. Sections 23 and 30, in particular, often bite on terrorism investigation and prosecution files. Aggregate statistical information that is already held in a retrievable form is more likely to be disclosable than case files, operational methods, or information about identifiable suspects. FOI is a transparency tool. It is not a ruling on whether particular words are criminal.

sections.title: Lawful routes to a reasoned ruling
sections.intro: There are procedures that do not require a person to attract a terrorism charge in order to ask the courts a legal question. None of them is a guaranteed route to a free-standing ruling on a particular phrase, and none of them is advice to bring a claim.

entries.title: Judicial review of prosecutorial guidance: the Purdy model

paragraphs.text: In R (Purdy) v Director of Public Prosecutions, decided on 30 July 2009, Debbie Purdy sought greater clarity about the risk of prosecution for a person who might assist her to travel abroad for an assisted death. The House of Lords held that, for the purposes of article 8, and the requirement that an interference be “in accordance with the law,” the Director should publish more specific offence-focused guidance so that a person in her position could foresee, to the extent the nature of the subject-matter allowed, the likely consequences of a course of conduct. The case is a procedural model for asking whether published prosecutorial policy is sufficiently foreseeable. It is not a template that can be copied, without more, onto section 12 and article 10. The underlying right was article 8, not article 10; the offence and the published guidance were different; and any analogous claim today would have to be framed in the light of the statutory text and of ABJ and BDN. Success is not guaranteed, and this page does not say that such a claim ought to be brought.

entries.title: Declarations, and a discrimination claim that would need evidence
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: The High Court can, in a properly constituted claim, grant a declaration of legal rights. English courts do not, however, sit to give advisory opinions on abstract or hypothetical questions. A person seeking a declaration about the criminal limits of particular speech would have to show a real legal controversy, a sufficient interest, and an appropriate defendant. Whether any particular publishing or educational activity would meet that threshold is a question for specialist advice on the facts. It is not answered here.

sources.locator: A concrete controversy and a proper defendant were essential even in the model case

paragraphs.text: A separate question would arise if there were evidence that the state treated materially equivalent expressions differently because of nationality, ethnicity or religion. Article 14 of the Convention, read with article 10, prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights. A claim of that kind would require comparative evidence of differential official treatment, not speculation about how different juries might have reacted to a defendant’s manner or identity. No such evidential record is offered or found on this page.

sources.locator: Article 14, read with article 10

entries.title: Deproscription, and an Attorney General’s Reference after an acquittal

paragraphs.text: The Jewish Network for Palestine application, already described, is an existing statutory route for challenging the listing of Hamas. It addresses the proscription itself, not the rules on how a jury should treat a particular form of words, and it is a different application from earlier deproscription efforts discussed elsewhere on this site. A refusal can be appealed to the Proscribed Organisations Appeal Commission, whose test is whether the refusal was flawed on judicial-review principles. Further appeal on a point of law is a later, limited step. That process may change the legal environment in which section 12 operates, but it is not a ruling on the Greenstein wording.

sources.locator: The 26 November 2026 application
The application mechanism
POAC appeal and the judicial-review standard

paragraphs.text: There is also a procedure that starts from an acquittal. Under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1972, where a person tried on indictment has been acquitted, the Attorney General may refer a point of law that has arisen in the case to the Court of Appeal, which must consider the point and give its opinion. A further reference to the Supreme Court is possible. Section 36(7) is explicit: a reference under the section shall not affect the trial or any acquittal in that trial. The defendant remains acquitted. The public, however, can obtain a reasoned statement of the law. The power belongs to the Attorney General, not to a private citizen. A search of public reports for this review has not located an Attorney General’s Reference arising from the Greenstein acquittal. That is not a finding that none was considered, only that none has been found in the public domain.

sections.title: A comparative record, rather than an experiment in public speech
sections.intro: If the aim is to understand how section 12 is being applied, the productive work is to collect comparable cases, not to generate a new defendant.

entries.title: What a useful record needs to keep

paragraphs.text: The speech-offences register already collects named and anonymised cases with dated outcomes, provisions and sources. A tighter comparative record of section 12 prosecutions would still need, for each case, the exact words alleged, the surrounding publication, the subsection charged, the mental element the prosecution said it could prove, what the police and the Crown Prosecution Service did, the trial court’s directions where they can lawfully be obtained, the verdict or other disposal, and whether a reasoned judgment exists. Anonymised identifiers used in other cases must not be joined up by inference. Trial transcripts and the judge’s directions in Greenstein remain outstanding, and they would be more informative than the verdict alone.

sections.title: The legal certainty paradox, named
sections.intro: When an acquittal establishes individual non-liability without establishing the general lawfulness of the underlying expression, other people remain unsure whether materially equivalent speech may expose them to prosecution.

entries.title: The principles in play, and the question that remains
entries.kind: Our analysis — not a judicial finding

paragraphs.text: Five principles are engaged. Article 7 requires that criminal liability be sufficiently foreseeable. Article 10 protects freedom of expression, subject to lawful and necessary restrictions. Article 14 prohibits discrimination in the enjoyment of Convention rights, including on grounds such as religion or national origin. Equality before the law requires that legal tests be applied without improper distinction. Legal certainty, in the broad sense used in this study, is the ability of a person to regulate their conduct in advance. Those principles do not decide that any particular phrase is lawful. They explain why an unexplained jury verdict is an incomplete answer to a citizen who is trying to stay on the right side of the line.

sources.locator: Articles 7, 10 and 14

paragraphs.text: The objective worth seeking is a reasoned judicial determination, not another unexplained verdict. Even a second acquittal, obtained by repeating the same words, might reproduce the very uncertainty this page is trying to describe. The strongest research question is therefore not “what would happen if someone else said it?” The strongest question is: how can a law-abiding citizen obtain authoritative clarification of the boundaries of criminalised speech without first having to risk criminal prosecution? The public in the United Kingdom is entitled to know, as far as the law can make known, what the rules on free speech are. The lawful ways of asking that question are the procedures set out above, a careful comparative record of real cases, and — if the Attorney General considers that a point of law arose in Greenstein — a reference that would leave the acquittal untouched.

sections.title: Limits of this review
sections.intro: Several documents that would tighten the analysis have not been obtained.

entries.title: What has not been seen, and what this page is not

paragraphs.text: This review has not obtained the Greenstein indictment, the posts and linked article as exhibited, the prosecution openings or consents, the judge’s legal directions, or a transcript of the evidence or speeches. It has not located a public Attorney General’s Reference arising from the acquittal. It has not independently inspected the Jewish Network for Palestine application file, only contemporaneous reporting of the filing and the statutory procedure. Official jury-research publications sometimes cited in this area were not verified from a live official text in this pass and are therefore not relied on. No Freedom of Information requests have been made for this review. The thought experiment is not a prediction of any verdict, not a finding about why the Greenstein jury acquitted, and not legal advice. It is not an invitation to publish the words discussed.
